extracted.intended_audience: physicists, meteorologists, physicians, instrument-makers, and observatory technicians (users and makers of thermometers)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and standards for establishing mercurial thermometer standards, calibrating and comparing thermometers (clinical and standards), and issuing certificates; includes apparatus, reading protocols, and packing/shipping guidance. Also contains procedural cautions and protocols for hypnotism experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass mercurial thermometers age-related change
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass mercurial thermometers slowly increase their freezing-point readings as their age increases after the heating they undergo in filling with mercury in their manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude of change may often be up to 1.5° F within two years; makers and users must account for age-related drift when treating instruments as standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling-point reading change with age/heating
rubrics_metrics.description: The readings of the boiling-points are also increased, but in a much less degree — perhaps not more than one fifth as much as the freezing-point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boiling-point shifts are smaller than freezing-point shifts; both must be considered when fixing scale endpoints after heating events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of heating on freezing-point (proportional rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the thermometer is heated at all, the freezing-point is lowered, and the amount of this depression is very nearly proportional to the square of the temperature to which the thermometer is heated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heating history matters nonlinearly; calibration protocols must control and record heating exposure to correct freezing-point depressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent vs temporary freezing-point distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: If a thermometer is kept at ordinary temperatures, the freezing-point indicated will be different than if kept at low temperature; temporary freezing-point (immediately after heating and cooling) gradually approaches the permanent freezing-point determined after some days at freezing conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference between permanent and temporary freezing-points is usually about 3/4° F. For standards, determine permanent freezing-point by long exposure (see standard definition) rather than relying on temporary post-heating values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling-point fixation and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: The boiling-point of water at the level of the sea, and with a barometric pressure of 760 mm. (reduced to 0° Cent.) at latitude 45°, is the second point in the thermometer scale to be fixed; the thermometer is exposed to steam of pure water and the true boiling-point computed from observed barometer, elevation and latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always compute and reduce observed boiling-point to the defined standard conditions (sea-level, 760 mm, latitude 45°) before fixing 100° C / 212° F on the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration by equal volumes (graduation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dividing of the tube so that an equal volume of mercury may occupy the same number of degrees at the various parts of the tube is called the calibration of a thermometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ordinary standards dividing by equal volumes is usual; for highest-class work graduate 0°–100° C into 100 equal parts and/or use a millimetre scale so observers can determine corrections at each degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration precision expectation (Kew standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision attained in calibration of standards when greatest care is exercised can be very high; in Yale's three Kew standards the maximum sum of errors depending on imperfect calibration is very nearly 0.01° in each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high-precision calibration methods (measurement of short mercury columns at multiple positions, dividing engine reference) to reach ~0.01° where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the theoretical mercurial standard thermometer
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theoretical mercurial standard thermometer ... is graduated by equal volumes upon a glass stem of the same dimensions and chemical constitution as the Kew standards 578 and 584. The permanent freezing-point is determined by an exposure of not less than forty-eight hours to melting ice, supposing the temperature of the standard has not been greater than 25° Cent. = 77° Fahr. during the preceding six months. The boiling-point is determined from the temperature of the steam of pure water at a barometric pressure of 760 mm. = 29.922 inches (reduced to 0° Cent.) at the level of the sea and in the latitude of 45°."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt these specific conditions when declaring an instrument referred to the Yale/Kew theoretical standard; align with International Commission of Weights and Measures conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator reading protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing thermometers in the water comparator, the thermometers are read as rapidly as possible, first from left to right and then from right to left. Two standards are read at the beginning and end of the series; if read at approximately equal intervals, the mean of the two readings will be free from the error of radiation caused by slow cooling or warming of the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read quickly and in both directions to cancel systematic positional/temporal biases; bracket runs with standards and use the mean of standards to correct for radiation and drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water comparator construction and agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an outer tank with an inner tank; admit water at controlled temperature, agitate thoroughly by a plunger until temperature is uniform, then allow agitation to subside before rapid readings. Disk accommodates multiple thermometers; thermometers attached by springs and read through a window (cathetometer used for precision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure uniform water temperature with controlled agitation and insulation; read only after agitation subsides; use cathetometer for fine readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation to prevent air currents
rubrics_metrics.description: The space between the outer and inner tanks is filled with cotton-wool picked until it has as little body as possible; the object is to prevent currents of air which would otherwise cause much greater conduction of heat to or from the water in the inner tank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cotton-wool or equivalent thermal insulation to suppress convective thermal exchange and stabilize comparator temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freezing-point apparatus procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Freezing-points of standards are determined in a cylindrical vessel with an inner vessel; finely crushed ice or snow placed so thermometers are fitted to corks embedded partly in the ice; use cathetometer for readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure close contact with melting ice for at least the specified durations to determine permanent freezing-point; prevent air currents with close-fitting covers; read with cathetometer for precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling-point apparatus and pressure control
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Regnault-style boiling apparatus (brass double chambers) or glass steam immersion for long thermometers; include manometer to note steam pressure difference and a standard barometer at same level wrapped for thermal stability; suspend thermometers with bulbs at prescribed position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pure water, equalized boiling (brass ribbon in tank), measure steam and ambient pressures, and reduce measured boiling temperature to standard conditions using barometer and location corrections; read with cathetometer when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer handling and co-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard barometer, wrapped in cotton-wool and cloth to prevent rapid change, is hung at the same level as the boiling-point apparatus, and the thermometers are read alternately with the barometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep barometer thermally stabilized and read together with thermometer measurements so boiling-point corrections can be accurately computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration of tube (graduation) measurement technique
rubrics_metrics.description: For calibration of tubes, mount two microscopes so the positions of the two ends of a short mercury-column may be read at the same time by means of eye-piece micrometers; dedicated comparator for this work recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure equal-volume lengths at multiple consecutive parts of the tube to compute the value of 1° at successive parts; use precise optical measurement for calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards comparison and foreign standards collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a collection of foreign standards (Kew, Seewarte, Imperial Commission, etc.) and use them to represent international work; compare important standards with recognized international observatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and compare against internationally recognized standards to ensure the observatory's standards are accurate copies of leading observatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different apparatus for clinical vs standards work
rubrics_metrics.description: For clinical thermometers a smaller apparatus on the same general principles is used; clinical work requires a much less degree of precision, the work may be simplified (no cathetometer; self-registering thermometers can be lifted to read).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match apparatus complexity to desired precision: simplified comparator acceptable for clinical thermometers; high-precision standards need full comparator and optical readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing and shipping instructions for thermometers
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermometers may be sent by mail or express directed to Winchester Observatory, New Haven; if by mail (and nothing larger than a clinical thermometer should be), they ought to be packed in a wooden box, in tissue-paper. A little care taken in packing them in soft paper will materially lessen the risk of accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mail large thermometers; use wooden box and tissue/soft paper; pack to minimize breakage during transit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates and turnaround time
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary thermometers are returned with certificates stating their deviation from the true mercurial standard for every ten degrees, within a few days from the date of their reception. Standards require from a week to a month for their investigation, depending upon degree of precision desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue certificates that report deviations at regular intervals (every 10°); communicate expected turnaround times to senders depending on whether instrument is ordinary or a standard requiring high precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation that makers supply certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no good reason why any maker should not furnish, with any thermometer sold, a certificate stating the errors of that particular instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers should provide per-instrument certificates of error to improve uniformity and trust in instrument readings (useful for organizations needing uniform data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading questions in hypnotic-memory testing
rubrics_metrics.description: In testing whether the hypnotic, after waking, remembers what has passed, it is important that he be not assisted by being asked a question the form of which will suggest the answer. If he is asked if he remembers any particular thing, his answer will always be 'Yes'; but if he is asked, generally, what has taken place, he will answer that he does not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral, non-suggestive questioning to assess memory in hypnotic subjects; avoid specific prompting which can elicit affirmative responses regardless of true memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of direction in magnetic passes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not, then, a matter of indifference whether we change the direction of the passes: we should persevere in the one which was adopted in the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing the direction of passes can dissipate the hypnotic effect; stick to the initially adopted direction during induction/maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution to avoid excessive motor-rigidity experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Great prudence is necessary in these experiments lest they be carried too far, and the respiratory muscles be affected. The rigidity of the muscles may be made so great in robust persons that it becomes extremely difficult to change the position of the limbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor respiratory muscles and overall safety; avoid producing rigidity that impairs breathing or requires dangerous handling (e.g., carrying by head and feet alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory modalities to induce hypnotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing sight on bright objects, certain feeble and monotonous sounds (e.g., ticking watch), and light and continuous excitations on the skin (passes) produce stupor/hypnotic sleep; different persons are more sensitive to touch, hearing, or sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select induction modality based on subject sensitivity; keep eyes closed or fixed gaze as appropriate; use monotony/light stimulation to promote hypnotic condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local reflex provocations via pressure/rubbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflex local movements are provoked by excitation of determinate points of the trunk: pressure between the fourth and seventh vertebrae makes him groan; pressure at the side of the last vertebra induces leg withdrawal; rubbing inside the thumb brings flexors into play, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific localized stimulations can produce predictable reflexes; apply carefully and with ethical/safety oversight; note that effects may be immediate and vary by individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory shock as a means to terminate hypnotic phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypnotic symptoms may be dissipated by suddenly changing the excitation: a slight shock on an affected limb, a cold object applied, or suddenly bringing light or sound, are enough to break the charm. Rigidity, if not intense, ceases on application of a cold body; touching the forehead or eyes with glass will make him open eyes while still sleeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To terminate unwanted hypnotic phenomena quickly, introduce a strong new sensation (cold, shock, sudden sound/light) or reverse the excitation; this is a practical safety/termination protocol.
